name: Debility of the Ulstermen
sources: Condren, Mary. The Serpent and the Goddess: Women, Religion and Power in Ancient Ireland. San Francisco: Harper & Row, 1989, 31–32. Cross, Tom Peete, and Clark Harris Slover, eds. Ancient Irish Tales. New York: Henry Holt and Co., 1936, 208.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Debility of the Ulstermen is an Irish mythological theme. The men of Ulster were cursed because a man mistreated his wife. The pregnant goddess Macha warned her mortal husband, the farmer Crunniuc, not to mention her when he went to the Assembly of Ulster. He boasted that she was swifter than the king's horses. A race was proposed, and Macha begged not to run so near to term. The king hoped her size would slow her, so the race went on. Macha won but died giving birth to twins. As she died she placed a curse on the men who caused her death. Whenever an enemy attacked, the Ulstermen would fall for four days and five nights in labor-like pain. The Curse of Macha lasted nine times nine generations and shaped the epic Táin Bó Cuailnge. Cúchulainn, born outside Ulster and free of the curse, held off the army of Connacht alone while the Ulstermen lay helpless.

okr.objective: Records Macha's curse, which laid the Ulstermen low before attacks, and its role in the Táin Bó Cuailnge.
key_results: Macha cursed Ulster after she was forced to race while pregnant and died in childbirth.
The curse made the Ulstermen fall for four days and five nights in labour-like pain at each attack.
The curse was to last nine times nine generations.
Cúchulainn, born outside Ulster and free of the curse, held off the enemy army alone.
